confidence_note: Verified in full text, ch. 4. The two daughters are an unnamed friend's children as Schwartz reports them; no names or ages beyond 'twelve-year-old' for the younger. Maximizer-unhappiness link is correlation, as Schwartz himself notes. The old claim that research shows maximizers make better decisions is dropped: the book only says they 'might do better objectively'.
facts: A friend of Schwartz and his wife fought with their style-conscious older daughter about clothes; they gave her a lump-sum clothing allowance and the arguments stopped.
They did the same with the younger daughter. The older, a satisficer, bought what she liked, often on impulse, without worrying about what she passed up.

The younger, a maximizer about clothing, felt anguish on each trip: was this the best use of her money, would she regret it two months later when seasons and styles changed. Schwartz: 'This was too much to ask of a twelve-year-old.' Her 'clothing liberation' gave much worry and little joy.
A maximizer can only know she has the best sweater by checking all the sweaters; a satisficer has standards, searches until something meets them, and stops.
The satisficer is not settling for mediocrity; she 'is content with the merely excellent as opposed to the absolute best'.
Herbert Simon introduced 'satisficing' in the 1950s and argued that once the costs of searching are counted, satisficing is the maximizing strategy.

Schwartz and colleagues built a 13-item survey scored 13 to 91 and gave it to several thousand people; those scoring 65 or more had depression scores in the borderline clinical range. He stresses this is correlation, not proven cause.
Maximizing is domain specific; nobody maximizes everything, so most people can satisfice more often.
scene_details: the younger girl asking whether she'll regret an item two months later when styles change
a survey item: 'I never settle for second best'
a score of 65 or more out of 91
tension: Two sisters get the same allowance and the same freedom; one enjoys it, the other is worn out by it.
opening_idea: Open on the clothing allowance that ended the fights with the older daughter and then failed with the younger.

lessons.idea: Set your 'good enough' standard before you start looking, so the search has an end.
lessons.anchor: The satisficer stops when something meets her standard; the younger daughter had no stopping point.

reflect_final: In which part of your life do you keep searching after you've found something that already meets your standard?

use_cases.situation: Child agonizing over spending birthday money
use_cases.move: Schwartz tells of a twelve-year-old for whom a clothing allowance meant worry; help the child name two things the item must do, then let them stop.

use_cases.situation: Colleague can't finalize a vendor after weeks
use_cases.move: Ask which vendor already meets every requirement and suggest signing that one.

use_cases.situation: You're on the fifth hotel comparison site
use_cases.move: Write your three must-haves, book the first that meets them, close the tabs.

pocket_idea: Write your standard before you shop; when something meets it, stop, like the sister who enjoyed her allowance.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: The same clothing allowance ended one sister's fights and gave the other only worry.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Friend's two daughters get a clothing allowance; older buys what she likes, younger agonizes over best use and regret; Schwartz: maximizer vs satisficer; maximizers on his scale reported less happiness.
